title: Full-Stack Python Web Apps with Reflex / Pynecone (PYTH_195_S1 to PYTH_195_S8)

slides.title: Pure Python Full-Stack Apps
slides.prompt: Frameworks like Reflex build single-page reactive web apps entirely in Python, translating Python state objects and UI components into React/Next.js frontend applications.

slides.title: State Class Inheritence
slides.prompt: Fill in the base class used to manage reactive application state in Reflex applications.

slides.title: Reactive Event Handlers
slides.prompt: How do UI components trigger backend updates in pure Python full-stack frameworks?
options: By binding UI events (e.g., `on_click`) directly to state class methods executed over WebSocket connections
By writing raw JavaScript script tags inside Python string templates
By sending periodic HTTP POST requests via page reloads
By executing C extension bindings on the client web browser
slides.correctAnswer: By binding UI events (e.g., `on_click`) directly to state class methods executed over WebSocket connections

slides.title: Reflex Button Component
slides.prompt: Fill in the Reflex component function used to render an interactive clickable button.
slides.codeSnippet:
def index():
    return rx.___( 'Click Me', on_click=State.increment )

slides.title: Reflex Architecture Compilation
slides.prompt: What output is generated when running `reflex build` or `reflex run`?
options: A compiled Next.js React frontend coupled with a FastAIPython backend service
A static HTML file containing embedded WebAssembly binaries
A native C++ desktop executable application
A standalone Android APK application bundle
slides.correctAnswer: A compiled Next.js React frontend coupled with a FastAIPython backend service
